statement: Missionaries and Kongo Christian intellectuals (including Afonso I himself) selected Nzambi a Mpungu as the Kikongo rendering of the Christian God, and nkisi was translated as "holy" — folding the Christian sacred into the same linguistic category as the traditional power-object concept rather than presenting it as categorically alien. This translation choice is traceable through the 1624 Kikongo catechism produced under Jesuit Mateus Cardoso (a now-lost 1557 Carmelite catechism preceded it). Cécile Fromont (The Art of Conversion, UNC Press, 2014; "Under the Sign of the Cross in the Kingdom of Kongo," RES: Anthropology and Aesthetics) documents the preexisting Kongo dikenga/yowa cross-shaped cosmogram as a genuine point of visual-cosmological convergence enabling Kongo Christians to read the Christian crucifix through an existing framework, producing elaborate hybrid crucifixes.

sources.citation: Fromont, Cécile. The Art of Conversion: Christian Visual Culture in the Kingdom of Kongo. University of North Carolina Press, 2014.
